source.title: Adversarial Training with Generated Data in High-Dimensional Regression: An Asymptotic Study

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the supplied text includes the paper and appendices. Figures are represented by captions and references, not their plotted contents.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own high-dimensional linear-regression results on risk as dimension grows, bearing on double descent beyond deep networks. This is a conceptual test in a different model setting and with adversarial-risk measures.
record.gate_note: The paper's own simulations and theory on risk versus dimension count. Double-descent findings cited from other studies are not recorded. Figure-only curve details are not inferable from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own simulations and asymptotic theory of risk against dimension ratio γ=d/n1 in ridgeless high-dimensional linear regression. It states that clean, vanilla adversarial and two-stage adversarial training all show double descent. That is a non-deep model class in a new setting (adversarial risk, pseudo-labelled data), bearing on V4. T3 fits better than T2 because the setting is new, not a new method aimed at the original question.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors report double descent in ridgeless two-stage adversarial (and clean and vanilla adversarial) linear regression, and say L2 regularization improves performance. They also derive a shortcut leave-one-out cross-validation formula for the two-stage method.
record.recipe_differences: This is an asymptotic and simulation study of high-dimensional linear regression, not a reproduction of the original deep-network experiments. It measures excess adversarial risk and includes a two-stage adversarial-training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk and the benefit of ridge regularization are examined under different penalty choices and attack strengths; Figure 5 reports that the optimal λ grows as attack strength increases.
record.peer_reviewed: 2nd AdvML Frontiers workshop at the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning; PMLR 202, 2023
record.problems: The numerical curve values and uncertainty bars are not available in the supplied figure-only material. The simulations use specified Gaussian linear-regression assumptions, and several sweeps use n2=∞; this is not evidence about deep networks, epochs, or sample-size increases.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for Figures 4 or 5: Figure 4 is described only as the theoretical counterpart to Figure 3, and Figure 5 concerns penalty selection versus attack strength rather than the tested double-descent curve versions.

untested.parts: No deep networks or model-size sweep.
n1 is fixed within the sweeps; sample size is not increased near the threshold.
Only linear regression under Gaussian assumptions is tested. The peak location (presumably γ=1) is not stated in the text.

Noise and variance are not varied, and multiple peaks are not examined. Whether optimal ridge removes the peak is not stated: the text says only that a proper penalty improves risk (r5–r8 cannot be determined).

record.verdict_notes: All curve evidence is figure-only, so verdicts rest on the authors' stated observations. The risk measured is excess adversarial risk, not standard test error, except the ϵ=0 clean group in Figure 3. The record's V6 'tested' status is not borne out: the text never says whether the peak disappears under the optimal penalty, so V6 gets no verdict.

versions.untested_parts: No deep networks or model-size sweep in deep networks.
The number of labeled samples is fixed within the reported sweeps; the paper does not test whether increasing sample size near interpolation raises test error.
The tested setting is high-dimensional linear regression under the paper's stated assumptions; other model classes and risk measures are not tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested as predicting peak location across axes.

The paper does not test whether label noise or variance drives the peak, or whether the curve splits into multiple peaks. It reports a comparison involving ridge regularization, but the supplied text does not establish whether optimal regularization removes the peak.
No alternative effective-parameter count is used to assess whether the curve becomes an ordinary U shape.
